title: Phase Descent: Identifying Error Lineage in Passive Correlators from Harmonic Phase Coherence
Phase Descent: Identifying Error Lineage in Passive Correlators from Harmonic Phase Coherence
text:
Abstract
Passive correlators recover signal overlap from the energy imbalance between complementary interference channels — a physical realization of the polarization identity. When the projections are phase-like, the output is cosine in the angular difference between detector settings, and any distortion generated by a single latent perturbation through a single nonlinearity produces angular Fourier harmonics satisfying \(\phi_n - n\phi_1 = 0 \pmod{\pi}\).
We call this property phase descent. It follows from the Chebyshev expansion of analytic functions on \([-1,1]\), but is, to our knowledge, new as a fault-lineage diagnostic. Phase descent partitions systematic errors into two structurally distinct classes — analyzer asymmetry produces phase-locked odd harmonics, while recombiner asymmetry produces phase-incoherent even harmonics plus a DC offset — enabling a calibration diagnostic that extracts fault type, fault severity, and its own validity bound from a single angular sweep.
Numerical experiments confirm phase-locking to within \(10^{-4}\) rad for analyzer errors up to 20% severity, while recombiner-induced inter-harmonic phases drift continuously with error magnitude. The underlying principle applies to any measurement architecture whose observable is well modeled as \(f(\cos(\theta - \theta_0))\).

title: Bell Violations as Three-Party Quadratic Conservation: A Classical Three-Phase Realization
Bell Violations as Three-Party Quadratic Conservation: A Classical Three-Phase Realization
text:
Abstract
The hierarchy of Bell-inequality violations arises from the algebraic order of the conservation law governing the correlated source. Linear conservation (momentum-type) produces correlations bounded by \(S = \sqrt{2}\), well within the classical Bell–CHSH limit. Quadratic conservation (power-, intensity-, or \(|\psi|^2\)-type) produces correlations that saturate the Tsirelson bound at \(S = 2\sqrt{2}\). The factor-of-two amplification in angular frequency — \(\cos(2\Delta\phi)\) versus \(\cos(\Delta\phi)\) — is the double-angle identity made physical.
We argue that the standard two-party CHSH framework is an incomplete accounting of an intrinsically three-party conservation law, with the third party identified as the zero-sequence mode of the Clarke decomposition: the energy carried by the field between measurement stations. We construct a classical three-phase analog — a passive linear front-end of four delta-LC tanks with a shared resonant core, a shot-trigger Born-rule detector, and a zero-sequence closure latch — and show by reduced-model simulation and a SPICE-driven realization that it reproduces Tsirelson-saturating CHSH (\(S \approx 2.828\), error 0.043; winner-law RMS error 0.013; decisive rate 99.5%; energy conservation 100%).
The construction is positioned relative to prequantum classical models (Khrennikov’s PCSFT, Spekkens, ’t Hooft, Bohmian mechanics).

title: Single-Parameter Gauge-Covariant Loop-Flow Control for Phase-Shifting Transformers and Meshed Converter Networks
Single-Parameter Gauge-Covariant Loop-Flow Control for Phase-Shifting Transformers and Meshed Converter Networks
text:
Abstract
An active-phase link element is a branch whose series phase offset is set independently of its endpoint bus angles: a phase-shifting transformer (PST), a UPFC or other FACTS device, a back-to-back voltage-source converter pair, a dual-active-bridge DC interface, or a grid-forming inverter in a meshed low-inertia fleet. Meshed networks containing such elements — the European transmission system and its PST-coordinated border flows being the largest deployed instance — carry a loop-level coordination degree of freedom currently managed by four layered mechanisms, none of which closes the loop-local, real-time gap between them.
The note identifies loop-flow coordination as an instance of the actuated-edge regime of cellular-sheaf coordination, and shows that the cycle-space dimension \(b_1(G) = m - n + c\) gives a tight two-sided bound on the number of scalar feedback parameters required to asymptotically stabilize the trivial-connection equilibrium — attained by a canonical per-cycle feedback law driven by the loop holonomy, the gauge-invariant observable identified physically with circulating reactive power.
